 Student loan defaults are surging, and the government wants to unleash the bill collectors

 Dan Levin

 Full story
 Some ten million Americans could soon see their wages garnished, tax returns seized, or more in a federal push to recoup delinquent student loan debt.
 According to reporting from The Washington Sun , the Trump administration is reportedly planning to aggressively pursue people who’ve defaulted on their federal student loans.
 In recent years, the government has had much more lenient policies on those who’ve defaulted, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Roughly 1 in 5 federal student loan borrowers are in default , meaning they are more than nine months behind on payments. That number spiked after the pandemic payment pause ended in 2025.
 Should the new plan come to fruition, several questions remain, including how it would work, any possible legal challenges and what impact this could have on the U.S. economy.
 The plan
 The report says the government’s first order of business will be to hire private debt collectors. That could happen as soon as November, but administration officials preferred to wait until after the midterm elections. Those collectors would then help the feds collect major financial penalties from those in default.
 “The first thing that we have to recognize is that nothing they’re proposing is new, and in fact, it is something that prior administrations from both sides have done and have failed at,” Bonnie Latreille, senior fellow at the Debt Collection Lab at Princeton University, told Straight Arrow.
 After payments were suspended in 2020, Congress attempted to restart them in 2023. Former President Joe Biden stepped in and essentially gave borrowers an on-ramp that protected them for another year.
 Then in 2025, the Trump administration announced default collections would resume but paused the plan in January. Two months later, the onus of collecting defaulted federal loans was shifted from the Education Department to the Treasury Department.
 “I think the only reason we haven’t really seen it get turned back on, before this is because of the transition to Treasury,” Betsy Mayotte, president of the Institute of Student Loan Advisors, told Straight Arrow.
 The U.S. Treasury Department Building is seen on Aug. 8, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Carter/Getty Images) 
 There’s big money at stake here. The government’s student loan portfolio is about $1.7 trillion, which, if that were a nation, would be the 17 th highest GDP in the world. $234 billion of that is in default . 
 And in some ways, the government is essentially required to pursue these debts. The Debt Collection Improvement Act of 1996 generally requires federal agencies to refer non-tax debts that are at least 180 days delinquent to the Treasury Department for collection, subject to statutory exceptions. For example, a federal government contract debt usually requires the feds to pursue the money within six years.
 However, for federal student loans, Congress authorized the government to pursue defaulted federal student loans without any statute of limitations.
 “We’ve set up a system with federal student loans where there’s no statute of limitations, and these loans can and often do follow people all the way to their grave, and where they’re quite difficult to discharge in bankruptcy,” Abby Shafroth, director of the student loan borrower assistance project at the National Consumer Law Center, told Straight Arrow.
 There is also reportedly some turmoil within the Trump administration on how to go about this. Some Treasury officials have raised concerns that aggressive collections could harm low-income borrowers. But some officials argue that delays cost taxpayers’ money to the tune of $5 billion so far.
 “From a policy perspective, people forget that these federal student loans are actually owed to the U.S. taxpayer,” Mayotte said. “That’s who your lender is: the U.S. taxpayer.”
 There’s no official timeline on this yet, but some officials are reportedly pushing to begin in the current tax year, which runs through April 15, 2027.
 The issues
 None of the experts Straight Arrow spoke with were overly fond of a plan involving involuntary debt collection, although all acknowledged it’s part of taking out a federal student loan.
 Many of their concerns centered on the communication to those borrowers, especially since this plan could start in the next few months.
 “I’m concerned to hear reports that they may be resuming collection of defaulted student loans in the next year, given that there hasn’t been any notice or warning to student loan borrowers,” Shafroth said. “There are roughly 10 million people with federal student loans in default. That’s a lot of people who could be facing surprise seizures of money that they’re counting on to pay their bills and make ends meet.”
 Part of that concern comes from the fact that it’s been more than half a decade since this has been an issue for borrowers.
 “It’s been so long since they’ve done it that borrowers didn’t realize that necessarily that it was a thing or didn’t think they were going to come back and necessarily start doing it again,” Mayotte said.
 Then, of course, there’s the concern about dipping into the pockets of people who are likely already struggling.
 Recent research shows many people fell behind on their federal loans because they simply could not afford the payments.
 “People don’t default on their loans for funsies,” Mayotte said. “They default because they’re struggling.”
 The other element that research found was that most people had no idea about other payment plans that were potentially available for them, and those options have significantly dwindled under the Trump administration.
 As of July 1, the Biden-era SAVE plan is gone. It’s been replaced with fewer plans, including a new income-driven plan and a tiered standard plan that could increase monthly payments for some borrowers and reduce available paths to affordable repayment.
 “The reality is now everyone is defaulting,” Latreille said. “The system is broken. People can’t switch repayment plans. They can’t find an affordable repayment option, and they’re being set up to fail.”
 Student loan borrowers hold a pop-up sit-in in then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy’s office to put borrowers over billionaires and stop the Default Creation Bill in the Rayburn House Office Building on April 25, 2023, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Paul Morigi/Getty Images for We the 45 Million) 
 Other concerns were over whether the government could handle any of this correctly. And that’s not just on the Trump administration. Once that pandemic pause went into effect, it triggered all kinds of immediate issues, including borrowers being incorrectly marked delinquent, collection payments continuing despite the pause, refund errors and more.
 During that time, the Education Department also transferred millions of student loan debt accounts between servicers, which was found to lead to guidance and accuracy issues.
 “You move a couch, you suddenly find all the things that are hidden under there,” Latreille said. “The loan transfers uncovered a bunch of errors.”
 The alternatives
 Unless you’re one of the mostly wealthy people or businesses that got a PPP loan during COVID, federal loans typically need to be repaid.
 As the Trump administration weighs this plan, they have launched a new portal less than a month ago. The Defaulted Loans Support Center gives borrowers with defaulted federal student loans an online path to get their loans back into good standing.
 Previously, that was a fairly complicated and, at times, archaic process that involved lengthy phone calls, paper forms and faxing documents.
 “We’ve worked with them on that,” Shafroth said. “I think that’s an important thing to have available, and it’s too bad that it took until 2026 to get an online way to manage student loans in default. This is a good first step, but very few people know about it yet.”
 That portal is located at studentaid.gov.
 It lets borrowers in default apply for loan rehabilitation online, apply to consolidate eligible loans, make payments, compare options and more.
 “When it comes to finances, that’s something people don’t like to talk about, especially if they’re delinquent or they’re struggling financially, there’s a lot of shame, there’s a lot of anxiety, there’s a lot of fear,” Mayotte said. “So, I think it’s a really positive step on behalf of the Treasury to make it so people don’t have to talk to somebody if they don’t want to.”
 There’s also the bigger issue at play here and that’s the cost of education in America.
 The U.S. has by far the most expensive average cost of public tuition for higher education. The average cost has risen nearly 84% since 2007.
 “Student loans are not the problem,” Mayotte said. “Student loans are a symptom of the problem. There was all kinds of talk in the last administration of doing broad student loan forgiveness, and I was a big fan of that, and I was as disappointed as everybody else when it didn’t go anywhere. But what I was also saying when they were talking about doing that was, that’s great, but it doesn’t solve the problem. The loans are just going to start building up again the day after they forgive them.”

 Why this
 story matters
Roughly 10 million Americans with defaulted federal student loans face the reported resumption of involuntary collection measures, including wage garnishment and tax refund seizure, with no official notice yet issued to borrowers.
 Wages and refunds at risk
 According to experts cited in the article, borrowers in default could face surprise seizures of wages or tax refunds, potentially without prior warning, if collections resume.
 Fewer repayment options now
 As of July 1, the Biden-era SAVE plan has been eliminated and replaced with fewer income-driven options, which the article says could increase monthly payments for some borrowers.
 New online portal available
 The Treasury Department launched a Defaulted Loans Support Center at studentaid.gov less than a month ago, giving borrowers an online path to rehabilitation, consolidation and payment options.
